questionStyle: Four independent English statements, select all correct, no number-of-correct-options hint; plausible mechanism or scope misconceptions.
curation: 28 principle- and application-led English questions. Numerical recall, case-value memorization and arithmetic are removed; Chinese explanations include per-option judgments, key English vocabulary and an explicit causal chain.
coverageMethod: Each inventory item names an actually tested proposition. testedBy stores exact option text, so it remains valid after publication rearranges option letters. A false proposition tests the corresponding misconception, corrected in its explanation.

topics.topic: Focused-electron scanning; comparison with scanning confocal microscopy

testedBy.optionText: SEM replaces the focused light beam of a scanning optical microscope with a focused electron beam.

topics.topic: High resolution, large depth of field and three-dimensional morphology; qualified performance claims

testedBy.optionText: Its spatial resolution and large depth of field are useful for studying rough surface morphology.
A surface image by itself determines both the topography and the complete elemental composition.

topics.topic: Morphology versus local chemical information and spectroscopy

testedBy.optionText: A BSE image provides the same quantitative chemical information as an elemental spectrum.

topics.topic: Electron acceleration, qualitative energy–wavelength relation

testedBy.optionText: Raising beam energy shortens the electron wavelength and improves the diffraction-only expectation.
The detector assigns every detected electron to the same physical point where it was generated, so lateral spreading cannot blur an image.

topics.topic: Rayleigh wavelength/NA dependence and qualitative trend versus practical resolution

testedBy.optionText: Raising beam energy shortens the electron wavelength and improves the diffraction-only expectation.
In a bulk specimen, higher-energy electrons can spread farther sideways before generating the measured signal.
A voltage setting must balance the wavelength benefit against the size of the signal-generating region.

topics.topic: SEM hardware roles: electron source, accelerator, condenser, objective, scan coils, detectors and readout

testedBy.optionText: Electron gun: supplies electrons; accelerator: sets beam energy and influences interaction depth.
Condenser lenses: control electron illumination; objective lens: controls focus and influences resolution.
Scan coils: control beam position and scanned area, thereby affecting magnification.
Detectors and readout: associate measured signal intensity with raster positions to construct the image.

topics.topic: Raster dwell, serial pixel acquisition, scan direction versus flyback and scan-speed/SNR trade-off

testedBy.optionText: The frame is assembled serially, although raster acquisition can still be fast.
A slower scan can improve signal-to-noise ratio by allowing more signal collection at each position.
In the illustrated raster, flyback contributes image data in the same way as the forward scan.
All raster positions must be exposed simultaneously before any pixel intensity is recorded.

topics.topic: Large-area exploration and navigation compared with SPM; scan-area magnification versus resolution

testedBy.optionText: Reducing the scanned specimen area at fixed display size increases magnification, without itself guaranteeing newly resolved detail.
SEM navigation is restricted to the same small fixed field in the way described for scanning-probe exploration.
Changing the scan area necessarily changes the kinetic energy of every electron.
Increasing displayed magnification alone removes the specimen interaction-volume limit.

topics.topic: Tutorial 4: beam current as electron delivery rate versus beam energy as kinetic energy

testedBy.optionText: Increasing current at fixed energy increases the electron arrival rate without changing what energy per electron means.
Beam energy concerns individual-electron kinetic energy; changing it can affect wavelength and surface sensitivity.
Increasing current and increasing accelerating voltage are interchangeable ways of shortening the wavelength.

topics.topic: Current–noise–damage trade-off; energy-dependent surface sensitivity

testedBy.optionText: Beam energy concerns individual-electron kinetic energy; changing it can affect wavelength and surface sensitivity.
Reducing current can reduce beam damage but may make the image noisier.

topics.topic: Tutorial 2: resolution balance between wavelength and lateral spreading in thick specimens

testedBy.optionText: For the same bulk material, increasing beam energy can increase penetration and lateral spreading.
The smallest interaction volume is the only factor that determines the final SEM resolution.

topics.topic: Interaction-volume depth/lateral spread versus beam energy and nuclear charge; qualitative energy-series chart

testedBy.optionText: For the same bulk material, increasing beam energy can increase penetration and lateral spreading.
A larger nuclear charge can deflect electrons more strongly and give a smaller interaction volume.
Changing specimen composition cannot change electron trajectories if the accelerating voltage is fixed.

topics.topic: SE source, excitation from specimen states, low energy, shallow escape and positive detector

testedBy.optionText: SE are low-energy specimen electrons that mainly escape from a shallow region near the surface.
SE are incident beam electrons elastically turned back near sample nuclei.
SE retain energies comparable to the primary beam and therefore directly sample the same deeper region as BSE.
The positive charge of the SE detector pushes secondary electrons away from it.

topics.topic: Tutorial 1: SE edge brightness from free-surface geometry; topography versus chemistry

testedBy.optionText: A larger fraction of the interaction region is close to an accessible free surface at an edge.
More low-energy SE can escape and reach the detector, producing topographic contrast.
The brightness proves that the edges must contain heavier elements than the flat regions.
Edge enhancement requires SE to escape directly from every point throughout the full primary-beam interaction volume.

topics.topic: BSE beam origin, nuclear electrostatic/elastic scattering, high energy and deeper source region

testedBy.optionText: BSE originate in the incident beam and can be turned back by strong interaction near specimen nuclei.
Their relatively high energies allow a deeper sampling region than the low-energy SE signal.
BSE are newly emitted valence electrons rather than incident electrons.
The nuclear backscattering process taught here requires almost all electron kinetic energy to be lost.

topics.topic: Tutorial 5: proton-number dependence of BSE chemical contrast; spectroscopy limitation

testedBy.optionText: A larger nuclear proton number can increase backscattering and produce composition-dependent intensity.
A single BSE grey value uniquely identifies an element without additional chemical information.
BSE contrast is chemical because the detected BSE are emitted from the core levels of sample atoms.

topics.topic: Same-region SE/BSE examples: Pt/ceramic and Ag/Au in SiO₂; complementary contrast

testedBy.optionText: SE and BSE images of the same region can emphasize different properties: surface shape and composition.

topics.topic: Beam-energy-dependent SE contrast and vanadium-oxide nanotube example; interaction versus escape depth

testedBy.optionText: Changing beam energy can change SE contrast without proving that the specimen topography changed.
Because SE directly escape only from a shallow layer, their image contrast cannot depend on the deeper interaction-volume changes caused by beam energy.

topics.topic: Depth of field versus aperture/convergence angle; distinction from penetration and lateral resolution

testedBy.optionText: A smaller aperture and convergence angle can increase depth of field.
Depth of field is defined by the deepest penetration point of the primary beam.

topics.topic: Grounding and conductive contact materials; carbon-tape powder support

testedBy.optionText: A grounded conductive base, connected using silver paint, graphite paint or carbon tape, can drain charge; carbon tape can also support powders.

topics.topic: Non-conducting bulk coating, carbon/metals and sputtering versus heavy-metal contrast staining

testedBy.optionText: Non-conductive bulk specimens often need a thin carbon or metal coating, commonly applied by sputter coating.
Polymer or biological specimens may require heavy-metal staining for useful contrast.

topics.topic: Dry/bulk/powder specimen forms and preventive height check

testedBy.optionText: Dry bulk and powder samples are usable, but specimen height should still be checked to avoid instrument damage.

topics.topic: Venting, gloves and vacuum cleanliness; chamber camera and rotating/moving stage

testedBy.optionText: Vent for specimen exchange and use gloves to help keep the vacuum environment clean.
Use the chamber camera and stage to position the sample relative to the objective, then pump down before imaging.

topics.topic: Vacuum to reduce electron–air scattering; low-magnification navigation and main alignment sequence

testedBy.optionText: Use the chamber camera and stage to position the sample relative to the objective, then pump down before imaging.
Begin with a low-magnification overview, center the region of interest, and perform voltage, focus, aperture and astigmatism adjustments.
A high-magnification image should replace the initial overview, because magnification alone guarantees safe specimen positioning.

topics.topic: Aperture alignment: rigid image shift through focus

testedBy.optionText: Rigid focus-dependent image shift calls for checking aperture centering.
The two symptoms establish the same fault, so aperture centering always replaces stigmator adjustment.
Ordinary refocusing alone removes the cause of both symptoms without any alignment change.

topics.topic: Astigmatism: perpendicular elongation; multipole stigmator and oval-to-circular beam correction

testedBy.optionText: Perpendicular elongations call for the stigmator, a multipole adjustment that reshapes an oval beam toward a circular beam.
The two symptoms establish the same fault, so aperture centering always replaces stigmator adjustment.
Ordinary refocusing alone removes the cause of both symptoms without any alignment change.

topics.topic: Butterfly case: optical survey, SEM finer detail and top/side-view three-dimensional light-diffusing structure

testedBy.optionText: Reflection light microscopy can provide an initial survey, while SEM reveals finer surface structure.
Views of fine three-dimensional structure can help investigate an optical function without directly identifying a pigment.

topics.topic: Butterfly case: carbon mounting, sputtered gold and charging-induced flicker

testedBy.optionText: A conductive contact and an appropriate thin coating can help charge leave a non-conductive specimen.
Accumulated negative charge attracts and stabilizes the negative electron beam.

topics.topic: Beam damage mechanisms: polymer deformation, heating and etching; lower-current remedy

testedBy.optionText: Polymer swelling or shrinkage, heating and etching can be beam damage; reducing beam current is the suggested remedy.

topics.topic: Hydrocarbon polymerization contamination, residue avoidance and distinguishing scanned-area artefacts

testedBy.optionText: A hydrocarbon residue can polymerize under irradiation, so avoiding organic residue addresses contamination.
A persistent dark patch does not by itself prove charging rather than contamination or physical damage.
Conductive grounding alone removes the organic residue responsible for irradiation-induced contamination.

topics.topic: Charging mechanism, scan distortion/flicker, conductive drainage versus ESEM neutralization

testedBy.optionText: Provide a path for accumulated electrons to leave, or use suitable ESEM charge neutralization when coating is unsuitable.
Switch from SE to BSE detection and assume that unchanged specimen preparation can no longer charge.
Treat the distortion as proof of aperture decentering, even if it is unrelated to changing focus.
Use conductive coating only to improve focus, because charge accumulation cannot deflect a beam.

topics.topic: ESEM local gas/ambient-capable specimen environment, evacuated column, pressure-limiting apertures and differential pumping

testedBy.optionText: Most of the column stays under vacuum, while pressure-limiting apertures and differential pumping allow gas near the sample.
The electron gun, column and sample must all be at unrestricted ambient pressure.
Pressure-limiting apertures actively pump away gas, so pumping between them is unnecessary.
ESEM succeeds by eliminating every interaction between electrons and gas molecules.

topics.topic: ESEM charge-neutralization chain: gas ionization by SE/BSE, ion signs, sample attraction and detector repulsion

testedBy.optionText: SE and BSE emitted from the specimen can ionize nearby gas and generate positive ions.
The negatively charged specimen attracts the positive ions.
The positive SE detector repels positive ions toward the specimen, helping them neutralize accumulated negative charge.
Negative gas ions must add more negative charge to the specimen for neutralization to occur.

topics.topic: Tutorial 3: ESEM versus light microscopy for high-resolution wet, vacuum-sensitive or uncoatable specimens

testedBy.optionText: In-situ observation of wet materials and real-time gas/liquid/solid interactions.
Observing uncoatable archaeological material when finer spatial detail than optical microscopy is required.
An insulating ceramic must always receive a metal coating even when effective ESEM ion neutralization is available.

topics.topic: ESEM applications: gas/liquid/solid dynamics, cement, archaeological samples, non-conducting ceramic and unstained copolymer

testedBy.optionText: In-situ observation of wet materials and real-time gas/liquid/solid interactions.
Observing uncoatable archaeological material when finer spatial detail than optical microscopy is required.
Imaging a non-conducting ceramic or the illustrated unstained di-block copolymer without the usual charging preparation.

topics.topic: ESEM NaCl hydration: same-area time sequence and water-related dynamics

testedBy.optionText: Repeated images of the same region can follow hydration or other gas–liquid–solid changes over time.

topics.topic: ESEM aqueous titania/AgNO₃ example: BSE sequence, beam-induced Ag reduction and measurement perturbation

testedBy.optionText: Electron-beam-induced reduction can produce metal deposits, so the observation may alter the process being observed.
Using ESEM ensures that an electron beam cannot cause a chemical transformation in liquid.
A BSE image sequence directly gives calibrated concentrations of every dissolved species.

topics.topic: Sensitivity–resolution overview: spot size versus concentration range and non-universal capability boundaries

testedBy.optionText: Analytical spot size and concentration detection range are separate performance dimensions; the smallest spot need not give the lowest detection limit.
Every boundary in the overview chart is a guaranteed specification for all instruments and samples.

topics.topic: Technique selection by desired morphology/chemistry information rather than magnification alone

testedBy.optionText: The desired information—surface shape, local composition or a real chemical characterization—matters in addition to spatial resolution.
The technique with the greatest displayed magnification must be optimal for every material and measurement.

topics.topic: Integrated interpretation: SE geometry, BSE chemistry, energy-dependent lateral blur and limits of intensity-only inference

testedBy.optionText: Edge geometry can enhance SE escape even where composition is uniform.
Composition-dependent backscattering can make an inclusion bright, but its exact identity still needs chemical evidence.
A shorter wavelength at higher voltage prevents lateral spreading from reducing image detail.
The different observations should be interpreted through their signal mechanisms rather than one universal brightness rule.

topics.topic: Method correlation: optical overview, SEM surface detail and large-area navigation versus scanning-probe exploration

testedBy.optionText: Use a light-microscope overview to locate a region before investigating finer surface detail with SEM.
Use SEM for large-area exploration with easy changes of position and magnification.
Assume a scanning-probe instrument and SEM offer the same ease of surveying a large specimen.
Choose the method with the largest displayed magnification without considering the required information.

topics.topic: Application: reducing current versus slower acquisition, useful signal and specimen damage

testedBy.optionText: A slower scan can collect more signal per position and improve signal-to-noise ratio.
Raising beam energy is identical to restoring the previous electron arrival rate.
Reducing current can protect the specimen, while the acquisition settings must still provide enough useful signal.
Increasing display magnification alone supplies the missing detected electrons.

topics.topic: Tutorial application: task-dependent ESEM versus light microscopy for wet, insulating and uncoatable samples

testedBy.optionText: The experiment needs spatial detail beyond light microscopy while preserving a suitable wet environment.
Gas near the specimen can support charge neutralization of an insulating surface.
The mere presence of water makes ESEM preferable even if an optical method already answers the question.
Choosing ESEM removes the need to consider what information the detector actually measures.

topics.topic: Mechanism-based diagnosis: conductive treatment does not remove contamination or all beam damage

testedBy.optionText: Improved charge drainage can reduce flicker without preventing all beam damage.
Hydrocarbon contamination can still polymerize under the beam, so cleanliness remains important.
A stable image proves that the specimen remains physically and chemically unchanged.
Charging, contamination and beam damage are different mechanisms and may need different remedies.

topics.topic: Application: rough-surface focus range versus signal sampling depth and display magnification

testedBy.optionText: A smaller convergence angle can increase the range of specimen heights that remain in focus.
A larger depth of field proves that the detected electrons come from deeper inside the specimen.
Changing from SE to BSE detection automatically brings all specimen heights into focus.
Increasing displayed magnification alone extends the physical range that remains in focus.

topics.topic: Application: material-dependent interaction volumes and backscattering at equal beam energy

testedBy.optionText: Equal accelerating voltage guarantees the same interaction volume in every specimen material.
Stronger deflection by nuclei with more protons can make the interaction volume smaller.
A material-dependent change in electron spreading can occur without a change in lens alignment.
A larger nuclear charge can influence both the interaction volume and the amount of backscattering.

topics.topic: Application: charge drainage versus gas-ion neutralization, coating constraints and chemical-information limits

testedBy.optionText: A suitable coating connected to ground can provide a route for accumulated charge to leave.
In ESEM, positive gas ions can neutralize negative charge on the irradiated surface.
Suitable ESEM conditions can be useful when the original surface must not receive a conductive coating.
Suppressing charging by either approach does not turn an intensity image into complete chemical characterization.

topics.topic: Application: a missing SE feature, finite signal sampling and choosing cross-sectional TEM for buried structure

testedBy.optionText: Its absence from the SE image proves that no such feature exists anywhere in the bulk specimen.
BSE can sample deeper than SE, but this does not guarantee access to a feature at any possible depth.
Increasing display magnification makes the SE signal directly sample the buried feature.
If the task requires a cross-sectional view of a buried layer, an appropriately prepared TEM specimen can address that different information need.
